blocks.text: That is, in those hot regions lying toward the rising sun, swarms of flies are more troublesome than in our lands, and destructive to flocks and to people; as can already be understood from what I cited from Roger in note 1. But I add the testimony of Job Ludolf, which J. D. MICHAELIS adduces in the treatise entitled Lex Mosaica Deut. XXII, 6. 7. ex historia naturali et moribus Aegyptiorum illustrata, which is the fourth in his Syntagma Commentationum secunda, Göttingen 1767, §. 3, note 15, p. 98: „Job Ludolf, an approved writer on Ethiopian affairs, used to relate that huge swarms of flies sometimes fall upon Ethiopia, to be feared by men and beasts alike; and that there is no other safety than for men and flocks to be gathered into a circle, and for a ring of brushwood placed around them to be set alight, since the flies cannot get past the flame and smoke. The beasts left in the field are consumed by the flies, and only the bones are left. The Jesuits saw this; they were at first amazed [III, 348] when the Ethiopians bade them flee, adding that the flies were coming; yet they fled, and afterwards recognized from the bones of the animals what a plague they had escaped. I would not vouch for all of this, for it may have been exaggerated; but that Ludolf related it I know on sure testimony, that of my father, who spent some months as a guest at the house and table of Job Ludolf.“ Thus Michaelis.

„How the flies brought pestilence, although Pliny does not record it, is nevertheless easy to conjecture. For the multitude of dying flies can infect the air with stench; and by settling on food and fouling it they can become the cause of putrid fevers and dysenteries. Thus DIO CASSIUS, book 68, §. 31 (p. 1145 of Reimarus's edition), reports that Trajan was forced to raise the siege of the city of the Agareni because dense swarms of flies settled on the food and filled everything with nausea. He is silent, indeed, about diseases arising from this; but the mere nuisance of flies would hardly, it seems, make a man like Trajan raise a siege and abandon an expedition. Dio's words are these: καὶ ὁπότε ἂν δειπνοιεν, μυιαι τοις βρωμασι καὶ τοις ποιμασι προσιζάνουσαι, δυσχερειας ἅπαντα ἐνεπίμπλων [kai hopote an deipnoien, myiai tois brōmasi kai tois poimasi prosizanousai, dyschereias hapanta enepimplōn].“ Thus Michaelis in the passage cited, note 17; he, moreover, takes the Myiagros worshipped as a god not for an idol but for a bird that feeds on flies, since it is mentioned among other birds held to be gods because they give help against plagues.
On Zeus Apomyius and Myiagrus SALMASIUS, Exercitt. Plinn. in Solin. p. 9. 10, should also be compared.
To JOSEPH SCALIGER in the Notes on the Fragmenta Selecta, which are at the end of the Emendatio Temporum, and in Chapter 1 of the Elenchus Trihaeresii.
